1086.title: Recapitulation
1086.hook: Irenaeus: Christ lives every stage of human life again, rightly, to heal it
1086.howItsDone: Christians who follow the church year walk through Christ's life each year, from his birth at Christmas through his childhood, ministry, death and resurrection, and Irenaeus is honored as a saint in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moral influence: a centurion who watched how someone loved, all the way to the end. Your line was love that changes us.

A baby who has to be fed. A boy who stays behind in the city and leaves his parents searching. A man the neighbors know as the carpenter. A grown man with friends, enemies, and a job to finish. That's Jesus, and also the stages a human life can pass through. Luke pauses on the in-between years with one line: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." He grew. He didn't arrive finished. An early bishop named Irenaeus thought those ordinary stages weren't a detour on the way to the cross. They were part of the rescue.
screen: `THE STAGES ARE PART OF THE RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Recapitulation means going over it again, from the top. Irenaeus was a bishop in Gaul, in what is now France, and he found the idea in a line in Ephesians: God's plan is to "gather together in one all things in Christ." The human story went wrong at its head, with Adam. So Christ comes as a new head and lives the story over again, this time rightly. Paul puts the two side by side: "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive." And to the Romans: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Irenaeus loved the matching details. A disobedience at a tree in the garden; an obedience on a tree outside Jerusalem. Eve tied a knot by her disobedience; he pictured Mary untying it by her obedience, her yes. And he went through the ages of life. Christ became an infant, he wrote, to make infants holy; a child for children; a young man for the young. Each stage, in his telling, Christ passed through and lived whole. So the cross isn't the only place where saving happens. The manger is too. The workbench is too. The hungry days in the desert are too. The cross and the empty tomb finish it. Like a song played again from the top: the same tune, but this time every note true.
screen: `GOING OVER IT AGAIN, FROM THE TOP.`
`IN ADAM ALL DIE, IN CHRIST ALL ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Name the stage of life you're in right now: starting out, in the thick of it, raising someone, caring for someone, slowing down, starting over. Ask what it's asking of you, patience, courage, letting go, and stay with the answer. If you pray, pray for this stage as one Christ has walked; if you don't, just let it be seen, all of it.
Recapitulation. Going over it again from the top: Irenaeus's picture of Christ living each stage of human life rightly, to heal it.
Your line: every age healed. The manger and the workbench count too. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1087.title: A real body raised
1087.hook: the churches hold the resurrection was bodily, not only a feeling
1087.howItsDone: Christians who say the Apostles' Creed in worship confess the resurrection of the body, the Nicene Creed looks for the resurrection of the dead, and Easter Sunday celebrates Christ's bodily rising from the tomb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, recapitulation: every stage of life lived again, rightly, from the manger to the cross. Your line was every age healed.

A piece of broiled fish, and some honeycomb. That's what's on the table in a room in Jerusalem, on the evening of the first Easter, in Luke's telling. The disciples are terrified. Jesus is standing among them, and they're sure they're seeing a spirit. So he asks a homely question: have you got anything here to eat? They hand him the fish, and Luke says, "he took it, and did eat before them." Ghosts don't eat supper. Day five hundred ninety sat at this same table. Today, the question underneath it.

These last days asked what the cross does. Today: what is Easter? Some people today describe the resurrection as a feeling: grief turning to hope, Jesus living on in memory. The Gospels insist on something harder. In Luke, Jesus says: "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." In John's Gospel, Thomas won't believe until he puts his finger in the wounds. After eight days, Jesus is there again: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands." The scars are still there. Raised, and recognizably the same body. And yet not simply a corpse come back. In John, he stands among them when the doors are shut. Two friends walk beside him on a road and don't recognize him at first. Paul tries to name it in his first letter to Corinth: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." Christian teachers have read a spiritual body not as a body made of mist, but as one wholly alive with God's Spirit: real, and new. And Paul won't treat this as a side detail: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." The old creeds confess that the dead will rise too; the Apostles' Creed calls it "the Resurrection of the body." Christians differ on how to picture a raised body. These texts all speak of a body.

Rest one hand in the other and feel the weight, the warmth, the lines in the palm, any scar you've collected. In the Easter story, the hands that were wounded are the ones raised; nothing is thrown away. If you pray, thank God for this body as it is; if you don't, just let it be here, and be noticed.
A real body raised. The churches' confession that Easter is about a body: touchable, scarred, eating fish, and made new.
Your line: a body, not a ghost. Scars and all. See you tomorrow.

1088.title: Justified by faith
1088.hook: Protestants stress being declared right with God by faith in Christ
1088.howItsDone: Lutheran, Reformed and evangelical churches preach justification by grace through faith as the heart of the gospel, and Lutherans and some other Protestants mark Reformation Day each year; Catholic teaching speaks of justification as a gift of grace that also makes a person righteous.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a real body raised: broiled fish, scarred hands, a body, not a ghost.

Night, and a man with no children. In Genesis, God brings Abram outside and says: look up. "Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them." So shall your descendants be. Abram has nothing to show for this promise. No baby, no plan, no proof. Just the sky. Then comes the single sentence Paul will later build a whole argument on: "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." In this scene he does nothing but trust. And it was counted.

To justify, in Paul's letters, is a courtroom word: a judge declaring someone in the right. Not making excuses for them. Pronouncing a verdict. Day three hundred nine met this briefly; today, the courtroom itself. Here's the startling line in Romans: God is the one "that justifieth the ungodly." Not the good. The ungodly. And how? In Paul's words, "his faith is counted for righteousness," like Abram under the stars. So Paul writes, "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The verdict comes first; peace follows. For the Protestant Reformers, this was the heart of it. Martin Luther said he had been terrified of a God who judges, until he read Romans and saw that God's righteousness was something given, not demanded. Their phrase was faith alone. Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Now the honest part. James, in the same Bible, says: "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only." Protestants read James as describing living faith, the kind that shows up in what you do. Catholics teach that God's justifying grace both declares and truly makes a person righteous, with faith working through love, as Paul tells the Galatians. Lutheran and Catholic leaders have signed a joint declaration sharing a basic understanding of justification, while still differing on details. Today's picture: a courtroom, and a verdict nobody earned.

Bring to mind something good in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, a morning, a second chance. Notice the urge to explain why you deserve it, or to pay it back right away, and let it go quiet, the way Abram looked at the sky with nothing in his hands. If you pray, thank God for it; if you don't, just say thank you, to no one in particular.
Justification. Being declared right with God, a verdict that Protestants stress is received by faith in Christ, as a gift.
Your line: declared right. Abram had only the sky, and it was counted. Rest well.

1089.title: Becoming like God
1089.hook: the Orthodox speak of salvation as union with God, like iron glowing in fire
1089.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of theosis as the goal of the Christian life, pursued through the sacraments, prayer such as the Jesus Prayer, fasting and love, and they celebrate the Transfiguration as a major feast, a sign of the light they hope to share.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification: Abram under the stars, and a verdict received as a gift. Your line was declared right.

A blacksmith pushes a bar of black iron into the coals and leaves it there. At first nothing seems to happen. Then a dull red creeps along it. Then orange. Then it glows so bright you can't tell where fire stops and iron begins. Pull it out, and it lights the room. Touch it, and it burns like fire. And yet it's still iron. It hasn't turned into fire. It has the fire all through it. Orthodox Christian teachers have reached for this picture to say what salvation finally is. Not only a verdict. A glow.
screen: `A BAR OF BLACK IRON IN THE COALS.`

segments.voice: Theosis is a Greek word: becoming godlike, sharing in God's own life. Yesterday asked how I can be right with God. This asks how I can be filled with God. Day one thousand eighty met a line from the second letter of Peter, and the Orthodox build on it: God has given promises "that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature." Partakers. Sharers. Exodus has a picture of it. Moses comes down the mountain after speaking with God, and "Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him." He didn't know. Still a man, and shining. Now the careful part. Becoming godlike never means becoming God. The iron never stops being iron. Orthodox teachers distinguish God's inner being, which no creature can share, from God's life and light, which God pours out freely. One old saying: what God is by nature, a person may become by grace. Where can you see this light? Orthodox Christians point to another mountain. When Jesus was transfigured, Matthew says, "his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." They see that light as a glimpse of where human life is headed. John's first letter keeps the ending open: "it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him." Western Christians have their own words for this hope, like union with God and seeing him face to face. The Orthodox say theosis, and picture it glowing.
screen: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit by a sunny window, light a candle, or turn toward a lamp, and let the light fall on your face and hands. You don't have to do anything to be warmed. If you pray, simply stay near God, the way iron stays in the coals; if you don't, let the light do its quiet work.
Theosis. The Orthodox word for salvation as union with God: sharing God's life and light, like iron glowing in fire, while staying iron.
Your line: iron in the fire. Still iron, full of fire. Until tomorrow.

1090.title: Grace and cooperation
1090.hook: Catholics stress grace that heals and lifts, and our free cooperation with it
1090.howItsDone: Catholics receive grace above all through the sacraments, such as baptism, confession and the Eucharist, and in the Angelus and the rosary they repeat Mary's words, be it done unto me according to thy word, as a pattern of saying yes to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, theosis: iron in the coals, glowing all through and still iron. Your line was iron in the fire.

Halfway through a sentence, Paul changes his mind about who did the work. Writing to the church in Corinth about his years on the road, he starts out sounding like a boast: "I laboured more abundantly than they all." Then he catches himself, right there on the page: "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." So which is it? Did Paul work harder than the other apostles, or did grace do it? He seems to say both, in one breath, and feels no need to choose. That little correction is a doorway into how Catholics talk about being saved.
screen: `YET NOT I, BUT THE GRACE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Grace is God's free gift of his own help and life. In Catholic teaching it always comes first. Nobody earns the start. But grace doesn't push a person around like a chess piece. It heals the will and lifts it, so the person can freely say yes, and keep saying it. That's cooperation: working together. Paul uses that very idea in his first letter to Corinth: "For we are labourers together with God." That's the shape of his correction: I worked hard, yet not I. Not half and half, like two people splitting a bill. More like a sail and the wind. The wind does the moving. The sail still has to be raised. Catholic teaching points to Mary as a picture of this. An angel brings her an astonishing message, and she asks a real question: "How shall this be?" Then she answers: "be it unto me according to thy word." Grace came to her first. Her yes was still her own. Augustine, in a sermon, put it in a way tradition still repeats: the God who made you without you will not justify you without you. Protestants, as we heard two days ago, stress that faith itself is a gift so no one can boast, and guard against anything that sounds like earning. Catholics answer that our yes is itself a fruit of grace. Both are protecting the same thing: it all starts with God.

Think of one gift you have and didn't make yourself: a steady hand, a good ear, a free hour this afternoon. In this teaching, that's a place grace has already been at work, so picture one person who could use it, and one small, real step for them. If you pray, offer that gift back to God and ask for help to use it; if you don't, just settle on the person and the step.
Grace and cooperation. God's gift comes first, healing and lifting the will, and the person freely works together with it.
Your line: grace and yes. The wind does the moving, and the sail still goes up. Same time tomorrow.

1091.title: Can you know?
1091.hook: some traditions stress confident assurance of salvation; others a humble hope
1091.howItsDone: Evangelical and Reformed churches teach believers that they can be assured of salvation through God's promises, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of a confident, humble hope, nourished by prayer and the sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace and cooperation: a sail and the wind, and Mary's yes. Your line was grace and yes.

Midnight, in a prison in Philippi. Two prisoners, Paul and Silas, are singing hymns in the dark with their feet in the stocks. Then the ground heaves. An earthquake throws the doors open and shakes the chains loose. The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and, sure his prisoners are gone, draws his sword, ready to end his own life. Paul shouts: we are all here. The jailer runs in with a light, falls down trembling, and asks: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Paul's answer is short. But some readers hear a second question under the jailer's: once I've answered, can I know?
screen: `WHAT MUST I DO TO BE SAVED?`

segments.voice: Assurance means a settled confidence: here, that you belong to God and are safe with him. Paul answers the jailer: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house." John's first letter says why it was written: "that ye may know that ye have eternal life." May know. And Paul, in Romans, runs through a list: death, life, angels, things present, things to come. None of it "shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Reformed, Methodist and evangelical churches stress this: you can rest in what God has promised, and know it. But the same Paul writes that he disciplines himself, "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." And to the Romans: "For we are saved by hope." Catholic teaching speaks of firm hope and real confidence in God's mercy, without claiming certainty about one's own final state, unless God reveals it. Orthodox teachers describe salvation as a road still being walked, and speak with humble hope rather than a settled claim. Some stress confidence, some humility; here is where they meet. John again: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." Whether a church says I know or I hope, neither is meant to run on fear. And the jailer? That same night, Acts says, he washed their wounds, set food before them, and rejoiced.

Notice where worry sits in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, and let it be. Breathe in one line from today, nothing shall be able to separate us, or no fear in love, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, rest in God's promise; if you don't, just rest, without solving anything first. If dark thoughts ever come close, as they did for the jailer, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Assurance. A settled confidence of belonging to God: for some churches a sure knowing, for others a humble hope.
Your line: trust, not fear. The jailer's night ended at a table. See you tomorrow.

1092.title: Growing holy
1092.hook: grace keeps growing a person; John Wesley even spoke of being made perfect in love
1092.howItsDone: Christians in many churches speak of sanctification as lifelong growth in holiness through prayer, scripture, worship and the sacraments; Methodist and Holiness churches also teach Wesley's hope of a heart made perfect in love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, assurance: a confident trust for some churches, a humble hope for others. Your line was trust, not fear.

"But grow in grace." They sit near the end of the second letter of Peter, and take something for granted. The readers already belong to God, and they're still unfinished. A kid who knows she's loved at home still has to learn to share the last cookie, to say sorry first, to tell the truth when a lie would be quicker. Being loved doesn't end the growing. It's where the growing starts. An English preacher named John Wesley, whose followers became the Methodists, pushed that growth a long way: he spoke of a heart made perfect in love.

Start with the word holy. In the Bible, holy often means set apart, belonging to God, the way a cup set aside for the altar is no longer just a kitchen cup. Paul writes to the Thessalonians: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification." So it's two things at once. You're set apart. Then, slowly, you become what you were set apart for. The churches picture that growth differently. Lutheran and Reformed Christians speak of being declared right with God by faith; being made holy is the lifelong work that follows, unfinished this side of death. Catholics speak of grace that heals and lifts, growing through the sacraments and free cooperation. The Orthodox word, theosis, pictures being drawn into God's own life. Then Wesley. He read Jesus's words in the Sermon on the Mount, "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect," and asked a plain question: would God command what could never happen? His answer was what he called Christian perfection. Not a life with no mistakes: in his own account, people made perfect in love still misjudge things and still need forgiveness. He meant a heart so full of love for God and neighbor that love runs the whole house, with no rooms kept back. Methodist and Holiness churches have taught a version of this. Other Christians think it promises too much for this life. Wesley leaned on yesterday's line from John: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." He heard a promise in it for this life.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll see soon, and choose one small thing you could do for them again and again: a real hello instead of a nod, letting them finish a sentence, a message that asks how they're actually doing. Growth, in this picture, is less a leap than a habit watered daily. If you pray, ask for grace to keep at it; if you don't, hold the person and the habit together.
Sanctification. Being made holy: set apart for God, then grown, slowly, into love.
Your line: perfect in love. Not flawless, just full of love. Rest well.
